tier_reason: The README states the +146% (vs std::sort, 496-byte structs, crossover above 152 bytes) and +28% (vs std::list::sort, types under 272 bytes) figures verbatim, but these are first-party averages with no compiler, flags, CPU model or element counts; the repo holds only a correctness test suite (plf_indiesort_test_suite.cpp has no timing code), and the benchmark page on plflib.org is EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the benchmark code and methodology could not be seen.

corrections.caveats: First-party README numbers only. The README gives no compiler, flags, CPU, element counts or standard library; the repo contains no benchmark code (plf_indiesort_test_suite.cpp is a correctness test with no timing). The methodology pages plflib.org/indiesort.htm and plflib.org/benchmarks_haswell_gcc.htm#sort were EGRESS_BLOCKED; a web search snippet (snippet only) says the benchmarks were run on a Haswell machine with GCC (so libstdc++ is likely but unconfirmed; exact CPU model and flags not seen). Older pages quoted '+130% ... vector with 496 byte structs' (and '~480 bytes'), so the headline figure has moved between releases (README now says +146%). The win only exists for large or non-trivially-movable element types (std::sort is faster below 152 bytes; std::list::sort is faster above 272 bytes), so the average depends on which sizes and element counts the benchmark includes. Extra temporary memory: N * sizeof(U) for random-access ranges, N * (sizeof(pointer) + sizeof(size_t)) otherwise.

notes: Real, active (last commit 2026-10-03), Zlib-licensed (LICENSE.md, OSI-approved), 25 stars, not a fork, not archived; claim matches README exactly. Shortcomings: first-party only, no benchmark code or methodology in the repo, plflib.org methodology blocked (snippet says Haswell + GCC), headline number changed from +130% to +146% across releases, speedup confined to element types larger than 152 bytes.
